nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-046.prompt: A newly diagnosed client with type 2 diabetes asks you to write a 1,200-calorie meal plan that 'treats the diabetes like a dietitian would.' What is the correct CPT action?

options.a: Decline the meal plan and refer them to an RD or their physician
options.b: Write the plan if they sign a waiver calling it educational only
options.c: Copy a public food-guide handout and add their insulin timing
options.d: Start intermittent fasting because it is a common wellness trend

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-046.explanation: Medical nutrition therapy for a diagnosed disease is outside NSCA-CPT scope. A trainer may share public, general healthy-eating ideas, but a calorie prescription meant to treat diabetes belongs with a registered dietitian or the client's physician. Refer rather than invent a clinical diet.

distractorExplanations.b: A waiver does not expand scope; writing a disease-treatment meal plan is still unauthorized practice of dietetics.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding insulin timing turns general nutrition talk into medical advice the CPT is not licensed to give.
distractorExplanations.d: Picking a fasting protocol to treat diabetes is still disease-specific nutrition therapy, not general wellness chat.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-047.prompt: Which first session most raises exertional rhabdomyolysis risk in a new client?

options.a: Familiar 3×8 goblet squats in a cool gym with a trained lifter
options.b: Forty-minute easy walking on a treadmill in an air-conditioned room
options.c: Novel all-out 200-rep leg work in a hot, poorly hydrated beginner
options.d: Heavy triples with 3-minute rests in an experienced strength athlete

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-047.explanation: Exertional rhabdomyolysis clusters after unaccustomed, high-volume (often eccentric) work, especially in heat and dehydration. Crushing a beginner with novel extreme volume is the classic trigger. Familiar moderate work, easy aerobic sessions, and heavy low-rep sets with full rest in trained people carry far lower risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Trained clients doing familiar moderate volume produce little novel muscle damage, so rhabdo risk stays low.
distractorExplanations.b: Low-intensity walking in a cool room does not create the muscle breakdown load linked to rhabdo.
distractorExplanations.d: Heavy low-rep work with long rest is high intensity but low total volume; rhabdo tracks extreme unaccustomed volume.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-048.prompt: A 16-week pregnant client wants to keep lifting with you and asks to start today. What is the best first step?

options.a: Keep long supine bench presses as the main lift after the first trimester
options.b: Stop all planned exercise until delivery so there is no training risk
options.c: Hold her heart rate under 140 bpm in every session no matter her fitness
options.d: Get physician clearance and follow current prenatal exercise guidance

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-048.explanation: Pregnancy is a special-population consult: obtain physician clearance and follow current prenatal guidelines (ACOG-style), including avoiding prolonged supine work after the first trimester and using RPE or talk-test intensity. Healthy clients are often encouraged to stay active once cleared—not parked until delivery or capped at an outdated 140 bpm rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Prolonged supine loading after the first trimester can compress the vena cava; it is not a default main lift.
distractorExplanations.b: Uncomplicated pregnancy is not an automatic stop-all-exercise order; clearance plus modified training is the path.
distractorExplanations.c: A fixed 140 bpm ceiling is outdated; current guidance uses effort and symptoms, not one heart-rate number.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-049.prompt: A client hands you a lipid panel and asks you to raise their statin dose because LDL is still high. What do you do?

options.a: Stay in scope: do not change meds; send them back to their clinician
options.b: Add one extra statin tablet if they already have the prescription bottle
options.c: Write a zero-fat meal plan so they can stop the statin on their own
options.d: Say the lab must be wrong because they have trained three days a week

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-049.explanation: Medication changes and lab interpretation for treatment are medical acts. The CPT documents the concern, continues safe training within clearance, and refers the client to the prescribing clinician. Do not titrate drugs, cancel prescriptions with a diet, or dismiss labs because the client trains.

distractorExplanations.b: Adjusting a prescribed dose is practicing medicine; having leftover tablets does not authorize it.
distractorExplanations.c: A therapeutic meal plan to replace a statin is medical nutrition therapy and still outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Training status does not invalidate a lipid panel; dismissing labs delays needed medical follow-up.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-050.prompt: A client wants to dump a loaded deadlift on a crowded platform. When is that a serious facility hazard?

options.a: Bumper plates are loaded and the drop zone looks reasonably empty from your view
options.b: People are walking through the bar path, so the dump cannot be controlled
options.c: The client prefers to drop rather than lower because their grip is tired
options.d: You are filming the set for their social media and need a dramatic finish

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-050.explanation: Platform safety is space management: a dropped bar is a projectile. If people occupy the landing path, the client must lower under control or wait. Bumper plates and a 'looks clear' glance do not authorize an uncontrolled dump when traffic is in the path.

distractorExplanations.a: Bumpers reduce floor damage but do not make a drop safe if someone can still enter the landing zone.
distractorExplanations.c: Grip fatigue is a programming issue; it does not justify launching a loaded bar into other members.
distractorExplanations.d: Content for a camera is not a safety exception; filming never outranks controlling the bar path.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-051.prompt: During an outdoor session at 95°F (35°C), a client becomes confused, hot, and stops sweating. What is the best action?

options.a: Have them jog a short cooldown lap so circulation can dump extra heat
options.b: Give salt tablets and keep working at a slower pace in the full sun
options.c: Stop, begin rapid cooling, and activate EMS for suspected heat stroke
options.d: Move into shade, sip cool water, and finish the remaining work sets

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-051.explanation: Altered mental status plus hot dry skin in extreme heat is a heat-stroke picture, a medical emergency. Stop exercise, cool aggressively (shade, cold water/ice if available), and activate EMS. Do not keep them moving or treat it as ordinary thirst.

distractorExplanations.a: Continued jogging adds metabolic heat when the client already cannot thermoregulate; it delays cooling and EMS.
distractorExplanations.b: Pushing work in the sun and chasing salt misses the emergency; heat stroke is not treated by finishing the session.
distractorExplanations.d: Shade and sips fit milder heat exhaustion with a clear, sweating athlete—not confusion and a dry, hot client.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-052.prompt: A client with untreated high blood pressure asks to take a high-dose caffeine pre-workout before every session. What is the best CPT response?

options.a: Allow up to 400 mg daily because that limit is safe for every adult
options.b: Prefer a branded pre-workout over coffee because the label lists the dose
options.c: Have them skip the blood-pressure medicine that day so stimulants do not stack
options.d: Keep stimulants conservative and send dosing questions to their clinician

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-052.explanation: Uncontrolled hypertension plus high-dose stimulants is a consult issue. The CPT stays conservative on pre-workout caffeine and refers dosing, stacking, and medication questions to the client's clinician. Population caffeine limits for healthy adults do not clear a high-risk client.

distractorExplanations.a: The ~400 mg healthy-adult figure does not apply as a free pass in untreated hypertension.
distractorExplanations.b: Labeled pre-workouts often stack caffeine with other stimulants; a label does not make them safer for high BP.
distractorExplanations.c: Telling a client to skip prescribed BP medication is outside scope and can raise pressure further.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-053.prompt: You are writing the floor emergency action plan for after-school sessions that include 16-year-old clients. Which elements belong in that EAP?

options.a: Who calls EMS, where the AED is posted, and how you reach a minor's parent
options.b: Who calls EMS plus a standing rule that you personally drive to the hospital
options.c: AED location reviewed at hire once, with no further drills or posted copies
options.d: A first-aid kit inventory and a requirement to phone the owner before EMS

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-053.explanation: A usable EAP assigns who activates EMS, where the AED and exits are, and how to notify a parent or guardian for a minor. It is written, posted, and rehearsed. Staff transport and calling an owner before EMS delay care and create liability.

distractorExplanations.b: Driving an ill client yourself delays ALS care and exposes you to transport liability; EMS is the assigned route.
distractorExplanations.c: A one-time hire briefing is not an EAP; staff must be able to find the AED under stress and rehearse the plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Owner-first phone trees waste minutes; EMS activation is an immediate assigned role, not a permission request.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-054.prompt: A new adult client wants to pull heavy deadlifts today. You have a PAR-Q+ and waiver, but you have not reviewed risks, benefits, or the right to stop. What is still missing?

options.a: Nothing more is needed; PAR-Q+ and the liability waiver already replace consent
options.b: Documented informed consent on risks, benefits, and the right to stop
options.c: Only a photo-release so you can post clips from this first heavy session
options.d: A written 12-week guarantee that they will add 40 pounds to the deadlift

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-054.explanation: Screening and a liability waiver are not the same as informed consent. Before high-risk loading, the client should understand reasonably foreseeable risks, expected benefits, alternatives, and that they may refuse or stop. Document that discussion.

distractorExplanations.a: PAR-Q+ flags medical risk and a waiver shifts some civil risk; neither explains the session so the client can consent.
distractorExplanations.c: A photo-release is a marketing document; it does not disclose training risks or obtain consent to lift.
distractorExplanations.d: Outcome guarantees are unethical and still leave the consent conversation about risk unsaid.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-055.prompt: A bar glances off a client's head during a missed jerk. They feel foggy and nauseated but never lost consciousness. What is the best action?

options.a: Sit 15 minutes on a bench, then finish the remaining accessory work
options.b: Continue lifting because they never lost consciousness after the contact
options.c: Stop the session and arrange prompt medical evaluation for concussion
options.d: Ice the scalp and switch to light machine work to complete the hour

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-055.explanation: Suspected head injury ends the session. Most concussions occur without loss of consciousness, and symptoms can evolve. The CPT stops training, monitors, and routes the client to medical evaluation rather than waiting out a quarter hour or finishing the block.

distractorExplanations.a: A short sit does not clear a brain injury; delayed symptoms are common and further work adds second-impact risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Absence of knockout does not rule out concussion; continuing after head contact is the wrong screen.
distractorExplanations.d: Ice treats a scalp bump, not a brain injury, and 'light' work still keeps a possibly concussed client training.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-056.prompt: A torn callus leaves blood on the deadlift platform. How should the spill be handled?

options.a: Wipe the plate with a dry paper towel so the next client can keep moving
options.b: Mop the iron with dish soap and water until the visible stain is gone
options.c: Give the client spray and towels so they clean their own blood spill
options.d: Use PPE and an approved disinfectant per the bloodborne-pathogen policy

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-056.explanation: Blood on a platform is a bloodborne-pathogen spill. Trained staff use gloves/PPE, an EPA-registered disinfectant (or the facility's listed agent), and proper disposal. Dry towels, soap-only mops, and handing cleanup to the client do not meet exposure-control policy.

distractorExplanations.a: A dry wipe leaves infectious material on a shared surface and skips PPE and disinfectant.
distractorExplanations.b: Soap removes soil but is not the required disinfectant step in a bloodborne-pathogen procedure.
distractorExplanations.c: Untrained clients should not be assigned BBP cleanup; staff follow the exposure-control plan.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-057.prompt: You want to film a 15-year-old client's lifts for a training log that may be shared in the gym's private app. What is required first?

options.a: Informed permission from the parent/guardian and the minor, per policy
options.b: Only the minor's verbal okay because they are the one being filmed
options.c: A social-media waiver signed by the minor after the session is posted
options.d: Nothing extra if the parent already signed the gym's adult liability form

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-057.explanation: Minors cannot give standalone informed consent for recording that may be stored or shared. Follow facility policy: parent/guardian permission plus the minor's assent, before filming. Adult liability waivers and after-the-fact minor signatures do not cover this.

distractorExplanations.b: A teenager's verbal okay is not a substitute for parent/guardian informed permission to record.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent must come before capture and posting; a minor cannot ratify a privacy breach after the fact.
distractorExplanations.d: A standard adult liability waiver addresses injury risk, not media consent for a minor.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-058.prompt: Two days after a novel high-volume leg session, a client reports cola-colored urine, severe muscle pain, and weakness. What should the CPT do?

options.a: Add a light flush circuit, extra water, and have them train through the pain
options.b: Stop training and refer now for medical evaluation of possible rhabdomyolysis
options.c: Add more eccentric volume because deep soreness means the work is landing
options.d: Recommend extra NSAIDs and schedule a harder lower-body day later this week

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-058.explanation: Dark tea- or cola-colored urine with out-of-proportion muscle pain and weakness after unaccustomed volume is a rhabdomyolysis red-flag cluster. The CPT stops exercise and refers for urgent medical evaluation. Hydration circuits, more eccentrics, or NSAIDs delay care and can worsen kidney risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Training through pigmenturia treats a medical emergency as ordinary soreness and delays a workup.
distractorExplanations.c: More eccentric load is how many rhabdo cases start; it is the opposite of the needed response.
distractorExplanations.d: NSAIDs can stress kidneys when muscle breakdown is already releasing myoglobin; this needs a clinician, not another hard day.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-059.prompt: A client asks you to coach the snatch. You have never been taught to teach Olympic lifts. What is the safe action?

options.a: Cue the snatch from a popular video and keep loads at 40% of their clean
options.b: Teach only PVC-pipe snatches until you feel more comfortable spotting
options.c: Decline to coach the snatch until qualified; refer out or get trained
options.d: Coach the full lift anyway if they already know it from a CrossFit class

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-059.explanation: Competence is a safety boundary. CPTs coach only skills they are qualified to teach and spot. Until you have education and practice in the snatch, decline, refer to a qualified coach, or get trained. Light loads, PVC, and the client's prior gym experience do not create your competence.

distractorExplanations.a: A video plus a light percentage is still coaching a high-skill lift you cannot reliably correct or catch.
distractorExplanations.b: PVC work still requires the coach to see and fix faults; discomfort is a signal to refer, not to improvise.
distractorExplanations.d: The client's CrossFit background does not replace the coach's ability to spot errors and failed reps.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-060.prompt: A client slips on a wet platform, catches themselves, and says they are fine. How should the incident be documented?

options.a: Skip any written report because no visible injury showed up at the moment
options.b: File the write-up within 30 days once you fully recall the sequence of events
options.c: Record your opinion that the client was careless and therefore at fault
options.d: Complete a same-day factual report with time, conditions, and actions taken

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-safety-060.explanation: Near-misses belong in the incident log. Write the same day: time, location, conditions (wet platform), what was seen, what was done (cleanup, client statement), and witnesses. Facts only—no blame narrative. Delayed or skipped reports lose detail when symptoms or claims appear later.

distractorExplanations.a: Pain and claims often show up after the session; near-misses without a bruise still get a report.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting weeks destroys credibility and memory; incident notes are completed while details are fresh.
distractorExplanations.c: Fault opinions do not belong in the record; stick to observable facts and statements.
